rules.title: Opening Strategy Repertoire
rules.requirement: Encode a selectable library of opening approaches: character entrance, antagonist entrance, relationship demonstration, catalyst, in-medias-res, flashback, flashforward, dream, puzzle, quiet power play, parallel action, iconic moment, concealed clue, and others from the notes.
rules.acceptance: author can choose, combine, or decline techniques; compiler reports purpose and downstream obligations, never rejects an original opening for not matching a template.

rules.title: Hook-Relevance Audit
rules.requirement: Differentiate a spectacular opening that honestly establishes the work's primary conflict from unrelated spectacle optimized for momentary attention.
rules.acceptance: map the opening event to later causal, emotional, or thematic consequences; flag disconnected prologues without demanding an explosion or immediate violence.

rules.title: Opening Baseline and Disturbance Selector
rules.requirement: Support violent immediate entry *and* calm-before-chaos, quiet dread, comic disarmament, or emotionally charged normalcy.
rules.acceptance: baseline, disruption, and changed reader expectation are identifiable when relevant; the system accepts quiet, atmospheric literary openings.

rules.title: Multi-Layer Genre Promise
rules.requirement: Represent what the first scene promises separately about genre, tone, protagonist, danger, mystery, and narrative perspective. This is an operational extension of B048, not a second promise ledger.
rules.acceptance: later scenes can be traced to each promise; intentional genre flips carry enough early signals to be fair.

rules.title: Early Orientation Without Exposition
rules.requirement: Track minimum scene coordinates—where, whose perspective, present action, local intention, what is knowable—while preserving mystery.
rules.acceptance: test-reader confusion about basic geography/chronology is distinguished from productive curiosity about a puzzle.

rules.title: Nonlinear Opening Disclosure Contract
rules.requirement: For flashforward, reverse chronology, first-person retrospective, dream, and unreliable-voice starts, specify what time/perspective the audience initially believes and which later scene reinterprets it.
rules.acceptance: temporal or viewpoint concealment is author-declared, not generated as accidental inconsistency.

rules.title: Character Entrance Through Choice
rules.requirement: Generate or analyze entrances where a meaningful decision, refusal, risk, competence, or revealing flaw establishes identity more effectively than biography or appearance.
rules.acceptance: the character's action predicts or complicates a later choice; appearance-only introductions are flagged for review, not universally prohibited.

rules.title: Power Entrance Without Violence
rules.requirement: Make antagonist or protagonist authority legible through changes they cause in other people's behavior, setting, resources, silence, and attention.
rules.acceptance: readers can identify a credible asymmetry before any exposition about rank or power.

rules.title: Opening Tone Inversion Design
rules.requirement: Construct deliberate contrast between an opening's apparent tone and the larger story's tone without mis-selling the work.
rules.acceptance: record the first incompatible cue, decisive reveal, and intended reader reinterpretation; require an early way to recognize the contrast retrospectively.

rules.title: Hidden-in-Plain-Sight Clue Contract
rules.requirement: Design an innocuous object, action, sound, or presence whose later significance is fair and reconstructable, with exposure and salience recorded.
rules.acceptance: readers given the reveal can locate the original clue without retroactive insertion; a twist depending on an unseen fact is flagged.

rules.title: Fair Red-Herring and Unreliable-Opening Protocol
rules.requirement: Distinguish a character's false belief, a deliberately misleading image, an unreliable speaker, and an authorial falsehood.
rules.acceptance: a later reveal changes interpretation without requiring unsupported sensory impossibility or breaking declared viewpoint rules.

rules.title: Set/Rise/Twist/Tie Action Model
rules.requirement: Offer the *Set–Rise–Twist–Tie* framework noted in the source as an optional way to structure a confrontation; keep its claimed cultural provenance unverified unless separately sourced.
rules.acceptance: a fight can use an alternative architecture and still pass if its decisions and consequences work.

rules.title: Credible Personal Stakes in Combat
rules.requirement: Separate magnitude of hypothetical loss from the character's believable attachment, exposure, and probability of loss.
rules.acceptance: the fight's stakes can be stated in one consequential, character-specific proposition; routine 'save the world' language alone is not treated as emotional power.

rules.title: Combat Agency and Objective Map
rules.requirement: For each combatant track the immediate objective, escape objective, restrictions, and how objectives change under pressure.
rules.acceptance: major moves can be tied to an intelligible tactical or emotional purpose; choreography that exists only for display is reported.

rules.title: Fight-Space Geometry and Access Graph
rules.requirement: Record exits, obstacles, cover, elevation, available weapons, sight lines, distances, and changing access during action.
rules.acceptance: no actor moves through an inaccessible route or exploits an object whose existence and position were not established.

rules.title: Action Viewpoint and Perception Limits
rules.requirement: Simulate which movements, threats, sounds, and injuries a viewpoint character can actually observe under speed, darkness, obstruction, noise, and cognitive load.
rules.acceptance: the narration does not silently grant omniscient tactical vision to a limited POV.

rules.title: Capability and Fatigue Continuity
rules.requirement: Carry established training, reach, strength, impairment, ammunition, exhaustion, and injury through exchanges and subsequent scenes.
rules.acceptance: repeated actions become harder or change meaning when the physical state changes; no unearned recovery or unlimited endurance.

rules.title: Objective-Driven Combat Reversals
rules.requirement: Make shifts in advantage result from attempts to obtain, keep, protect, escape, or sacrifice something—not interchangeable blows.
rules.acceptance: each reversal changes what at least one combatant can realistically achieve next.

rules.title: Repeated-Move Adaptation Test
rules.requirement: If a signature maneuver recurs, track whether the opponent has learned, the environment changed, the timing differs, or the repetition is a deliberate motif.
rules.acceptance: an identical move cannot produce identical surprise forever without a causal explanation.

rules.title: Tactical Breather with New Information
rules.requirement: Use pauses, circling, repositioning, and silence to reveal competence, geography, fear, injury, or a changed plan.
rules.acceptance: the break changes the audience's combat forecast; do not insert pauses solely to match a numeric formula.

rules.title: Earned Environmental Twist
rules.requirement: Permit a previously established object, skill, vulnerability, rule, or change in terrain to invert the fight.
rules.acceptance: the twist has a visible precondition and does not introduce a convenient new tool without setup.

rules.title: Combat Detail Compression by Medium
rules.requirement: Distinguish prose fiction from screenplay action lines. Render selected decisive exchanges at high resolution while compressing repetitive movements; avoid demanding complete blow-by-blow action.
rules.acceptance: physical causality remains legible after compression and novelistic interiority is not stripped to imitate scripts.

rules.title: Dialogue Under Physical Stress
rules.requirement: Make fight speech serve motivation, distraction, bargaining, provocation, surrender, humor, or an earned callback, subject to realistic breath, pain, distance, and danger.
rules.acceptance: remove a line and test whether the fight's intention or relationship changes; do not require silence in every realistic fight.

rules.title: Action Soundscape and Rhythmic Restraint
rules.requirement: Use silence, impact, interruption, and selective sound words to orient the reader, not to saturate pages with capitalized effects or ellipses.
rules.acceptance: rhythm improves in read-aloud comparison without an automatic onomatopoeia quota.

rules.title: Fight Resolution as Character and Plot Turn
rules.requirement: Separate winning the physical exchange from achieving the scene goal and from proving character change.
rules.acceptance: the result alters at least one of capacity, relationship, information, moral commitment, or subsequent plot; action for its own sake is flagged.

rules.title: Antagonist Pressure Network
rules.requirement: Model antagonism as multiple agents, institutions, social norms, environments, or internal contradictions rather than requiring one villain in every story.
rules.acceptance: causal responsibility for opposition can be assigned without inventing a personalized evildoer.

rules.title: Mirror-Villain Divergence Map
rules.requirement: Track traits, experiences, convictions, and methods shared by protagonist and antagonist, then document the consequential choices where they diverge.
rules.acceptance: similarity alters at least one decision or moral dilemma instead of existing only as an explanatory parallel.

rules.title: Antagonist as Moral Stress Test
rules.requirement: Design antagonist actions that credibly test the protagonist's declared boundaries and identity.
rules.acceptance: the attempted test has feasible mechanics, more than one meaningful option, and consequences not resolved by author fiat.

rules.title: Looming-Threat Presence Budget
rules.requirement: Support antagonists who remain physically absent while their actions shape characters' options and expectations.
rules.acceptance: threat remains causally active via evidence and behavior; absence alone is not treated as mystery.

rules.title: Aftermath-as-Adversary Evidence
rules.requirement: Establish villain competence and severity through specific observable consequences, not only fearful testimony or ominous labels.
rules.acceptance: each indirect appearance teaches the reader something new about method, limits, or stakes.

rules.title: Secondhand Testimony Reliability Graph
rules.requirement: Separate what witnesses saw, heard, inferred, exaggerated, or deliberately concealed about a threat.
rules.acceptance: contradictory testimony can coexist without arbitrary omniscient adjudication, and a later reveal is grounded in knowable evidence.

rules.title: Motive Reveal Exposure Ladder
rules.requirement: Plan staged revelations of an antagonist's motive, from observable aim through rationalization to underlying desire, without automatically treating an ambiguous motive as unfinished writing.
rules.acceptance: later motive revelations reinterpret earlier action without contradicting known opportunity or resources.

rules.title: Heroism/Morality/POV Multiaxis Model
rules.requirement: Distinguish protagonist status, antagonistic function, sympathetic understanding, ethical conduct, and desired outcome for antiheroes, antivillains, villain protagonists, and conventional villains.
rules.acceptance: the model does not classify every self-interested lead as evil or equate reader sympathy with moral endorsement.

rules.title: Harm and Sympathy Coexistence
rules.requirement: Preserve a villain's credible attachments, vulnerabilities, virtues, or injustice suffered while accounting for actual harm.
rules.acceptance: sympathetic backstory cannot erase victim consequences or force readers to agree with the villain.

rules.title: Mentor-Mask Antagonism
rules.requirement: Support villains who first function as guide, ally, patron, or rescuer and exploit trust to advance another purpose.
rules.acceptance: the relationship has useful genuine actions and planted contradictions; the reveal alters past-scene interpretation, not merely a label.

rules.title: Greater-Good Rationalization Ledger
rules.requirement: Track the antagonist's stated objective, internal standard of success, sacrifices imposed on others, and the beneficiaries who allegedly justify those costs.
rules.acceptance: critique and consequence remain available even if the antagonist's plan works technically.

rules.title: Private Psychological Utility Behind Public Mission
rules.requirement: Differentiate a mastermind's announced social or political project from intimate needs for recognition, control, validation, belonging, or revenge.
rules.acceptance: this divergence predicts behavior at meaningful moments and can be contradicted by actions.

rules.title: Villain Archetype Composition Without Type Lock
rules.requirement: Make beast, bully, machine, mastermind, fanatic, henchperson, mirror, anti-villain and related models composable *descriptions*, not exclusive personality types.
rules.acceptance: a hybrid antagonist is representable and their decisions arise from the established character, not a stereotype.

rules.title: Scene Pledge/Contract Graph
rules.requirement: At an opening or early dialogue exchange, allow a question, offer, risk, withheld explanation, or promise to obligate later dramatic delivery. Extend B019's mystery ledger with scene-specific intention, due point, and payout mode.
rules.acceptance: neither trivial bait nor an entirely unrelated answer counts as payment.

rules.title: Suspenseful Conversation as Action
rules.requirement: Treat dialogue turns as bids to extract information, test a lie, change power, control time, obtain consent, or conceal a plan.
rules.acceptance: a long conversation has shifting positions and an altered end state even without overt physical action.

rules.title: Reader-Knows-Danger-First Mode
rules.requirement: Provide controlled dramatic irony in which the reader knows a specific danger before the threatened characters do. This specializes B017's information-asymmetry model for suspense.
rules.acceptance: readers can state the approaching consequence while characters have credible reasons not to act yet.

rules.title: Suspense Certainty Ramp
rules.requirement: Track whether successive details raise or lower the plausibility of a feared outcome, rather than escalating solely through louder prose.
rules.acceptance: a before/after reader forecast identifies what new fact changed the inferred odds.

rules.title: Conversational Subtext Intent Contract
rules.requirement: Represent what a speaker says, privately wants, believes the listener knows, and tries to induce.
rules.acceptance: surface politeness and hidden threat yield intelligible tactics and a causal audience payoff.

rules.title: Politeness as Constraint and Threat
rules.requirement: Model scenes where etiquette, dependence, hospitality, professionalism, or social roles make direct refusal dangerous.
rules.acceptance: the social cost of breaking the performance is shown; formal civility alone does not count as menace.

rules.title: Suspense Clock Semantics
rules.requirement: Separate an explicit countdown from implicit clocks (arrival, exposure, loss of trust, a decision deadline, diminishing options) with traceable expiry conditions.
rules.acceptance: the time pressure changes character choices; invented countdowns with no causal force are rejected.

rules.title: Meaningful Silence and Delay
rules.requirement: Distinguish waiting that permits discovery, grants power, raises vulnerability, or causes a cost from delay that merely pads a chapter.
rules.acceptance: shortening the pause would change suspense, information, or a choice.

rules.title: Reader Forecast and Emotional Participation
rules.requirement: Make a testable prediction about what attentive readers fear, hope, or suspect at selected beats, then compare with real reader reports.
rules.acceptance: the system reports reader disagreement and uncertainty instead of manufacturing a single validated reaction.

rules.title: Hierarchical Goal/Sequence Graph
rules.requirement: Model scene goal → sequence goal → act goal → novel goal, including goal ownership, time bounds, dependencies, and conflicts.
rules.acceptance: the analyst can show why each sequence exists and how local results affect the higher objective.

rules.title: Local Outcome Vector for Every Sequence
rules.requirement: Track objective achieved, resource cost, information gained, relationships harmed, villain benefit, and future options rather than one binary success flag.
rules.acceptance: a sequence can be locally successful and globally disastrous without label contradiction.

rules.title: Perceived-Now Versus Revealed-Later Result
rules.requirement: Record a character's and reader's judgment at the time of a supposed victory separately from later evidence that it served the opponent.
rules.acceptance: later revelations supersede interpretation without rewriting what the characters could know earlier.

rules.title: Interlocking Opponent Goal Simulation
rules.requirement: Compare protagonist and antagonist intentions at each sequence and evaluate how either side can exploit the other's action.
rules.acceptance: at least one nontrivial alternate opponent response is examined before claiming an intricate trap robust.

rules.title: Causal Goal Substitution
rules.requirement: When one opponent's action changes the main goal—from dismantling an institution to neutralizing a specific threat, for example—preserve the causal transition and abandoned obligations.
rules.acceptance: the new goal doesn't materialize merely because a new act has begun.

rules.title: Twist Dependency Audit
rules.requirement: Every major plot reversal must list necessary earlier events, knowledge, access, resources, timing, and chance conditions.
rules.acceptance: removing one required condition either changes the outcome or exposes an alternative route; unsupported guarantees are flagged.

rules.title: Bounded Antagonist Foresight
rules.requirement: Disallow mastermind plans that depend on perfect predictions of independent human choices unless the mechanism for control or prediction has been established.
rules.acceptance: test the plan against plausible deviations and identify which contingencies genuinely existed.

rules.title: Coincidence and Logistical Burden Audit
rules.requirement: Track how people obtained tools, traveled, concealed operations, arranged complex events, and survived unexpected obstacles.
rules.acceptance: plot-important coincidences or invisible logistics are explicitly reviewed; not every off-page routine requires dramatization.

rules.title: Complexity and Comprehension Budget
rules.requirement: Distinguish productive complexity from a plot that outruns the reader's ability to understand causes and stakes.
rules.acceptance: sample readers can reconstruct the major cause-and-effect chain at appropriate checkpoints without having to consult a wiki.

rules.title: Reversal Cost and Aftermath Persistence
rules.requirement: When a win masks a setback, maintain both outcomes in the event graph and carry consequences forward.
rules.acceptance: later chapters recognize the sacrificed person, compromised institution, depleted capability, or antagonist advantage; a subsequent triumph cannot erase it without causal repair.

rules.title: Responsible Sensory and Cultural Specificity
rules.requirement: Provide reference-assisted descriptions of sound, physical appearance, regional folklore, and setting while reviewing objectification, reductive portrayal, and misuse of living cultural traditions.
rules.acceptance: culturally specific source claims are attributed and reviewed; no arbitrary skin-tone metaphors or copied stock descriptors are required.

rules.title: Domain Verisimilitude With Freshness Checks
rules.requirement: For military maneuvers, policing, institutions, geography, equipment, physics, and similar factual backgrounds, ground concrete operational details in appropriate sources and note time dependence.
rules.acceptance: a historical list of FBI investigation programs is not promoted to a current federal claim merely because it appears in a personal research notebook.

rules.title: Cross-Medium Narrative Equivalence
rules.requirement: Preserve the dramatic purpose of a scene when adapting a novel to screenplay, audio drama, comic, game, or screen-based narrative, but recompute permissible techniques, pacing, and audience access to information.
rules.acceptance: screenplay assumptions such as page-to-minute ratios or capitalized impact sounds do not become mandatory rules for literary prose; the same core decision and consequence remain traceable.
